# How to Plan and Build a Product Demo Video with an AI Avatar

> **In short:** D-ID's official guide says a product demo works best when it shows one user problem, shows the product solving it, and ends with one clear next step. An AI avatar can deliver the narration from a script, so you can revise it without filming again. The product footage still needs updating when your screens change.

If you have ever tried to explain a product to a friend over text, you know how quickly the message gets lost. A short video can do that job better, but filming a presenter, booking a room and re-recording every time a price line or button changes is a lot of work. This guide walks through a workflow for building a demo with an AI avatar, a computer-generated on-screen presenter, and keeping it up to date.

## What you need before you start

Before you begin, gather three things:

- **A product or workflow to show.** This can be a web app, a software tool or a process your team runs on a computer.
- **A specific user.** A support lead, a new hire or a small shop owner is more useful than "everyone."
- **A tool that can generate an AI avatar video.** D-ID's official guide uses D-ID Studio as its example. The principles below work with any tool that turns a script into a presenter.

You do not need a camera or a studio. You do need a way to capture your screen, which most computers can do with built-in or free tools.

## Step 1 — Pick one audience and one task

Start by naming one person and one job they need to finish. The official guide recommends building each demo around one audience, one task and one outcome. Everything else in the video should serve that goal.

Write a sentence like this on a notepad:

💬 *"A support lead sets up an escalation rule so urgent tickets reach the right person within an hour."*

You'll know it worked when you can describe the viewer and the result in one sentence without the word "and" appearing more than once.

## Step 2 — Outline the scenes

Next, sketch the video as three parts: the problem, the product solving it, and the next step. Keep the outline short. Think of it as a rough map, not a full script.

A simple outline might look like this:

- **Scene 1, the problem:** Urgent tickets sit in a general queue for hours.
- **Scene 2, the solution:** The escalation rule is set, and the urgent ticket moves to the right person.
- **Scene 3, the next step:** Visit the setup page to create your first rule.

Wistia's video research, which the guide cites, suggests that how-to and product demo videos meant to explain things often land in a range of about one to five minutes. Use that as a starting point, not a strict rule. A technical evaluator may watch longer, while a social clip may need to be shorter.

You'll know it worked when each scene has one job and you can say what the viewer should feel or know at the end of it.

## Step 3 — Record the product footage

The product footage is the part of the video that shows the real software. The guide is clear that this is a separate job from the avatar. If your screens are recorded from the real product, the footage must match what viewers will see.

Use a screen recording tool on your computer. Some tips from the guide:

- **Move the cursor slowly and on purpose.** Viewers need time to read labels and follow each click.
- **Zoom in on small interface elements** so the text is readable on a phone.
- **Record the real task**, not a feature tour. Stick to the steps in Scene 2.

Record a few seconds longer than you think you need at the start and end of each clip. That gives you room to trim later.

You'll know it worked when someone who has never seen the product can follow each click without pausing the video.

## Step 4 — Write the narration, one scene at a time

The avatar will speak your words, so write them in plain, conversational sentences. Read them out loud once you finish. If you stumble, your viewer will hear the stumble too.

Write narration for each scene separately. That way, you can swap or fix one scene without rewriting the whole script.

💬 *"Urgent tickets used to wait in the general queue. Now, one rule sends them straight to the right person. Here's how it looks."*

Keep each sentence short enough to say in one breath. If a technical term appears, such as "escalation rule" (a setting that automatically passes a request to someone more senior), explain it in a few words the first time you use it.

You'll know it worked when you can read each scene aloud in about the time the footage takes to play.

## Step 5 — Choose the presenter and the voice

Pick a presenter that looks professional for your audience and a voice that matches your brand. The guide notes that an avatar lets you change the script, voice, presenter, language, background or visual content and generate a new version without filming.

Think about placement too. The presenter should support the footage, not cover it. Put the avatar in a corner or a clear area so the viewer can still see the buttons and labels.

💬 *"Keep the presenter small in the lower-right corner, and leave the main screen unobstructed."*

If you plan to offer the video in more than one language, the guide says D-ID creates videos in more than 120 languages and accents while keeping the same presenter. Plan for translation, a review by a native speaker and any changes to on-screen text.

You'll know it worked when a test viewer can read the labels on screen and still hear and see the presenter clearly.

## Step 6 — Assemble, generate and review

Put the footage and the avatar together, then generate the video. Watch the full result from start to finish, not just the parts you changed.

Check for these things:

- The footage matches the product as it looks today.
- The narration lines up with each click.
- The call to action is the only next step at the end.

If you need to change a sentence, edit the script and regenerate the presenter. If the interface changed, re-record only the affected screen clip. The guide makes this distinction: the avatar saves you a presenter reshoot, but the footage update is still yours.

You'll know it worked when a colleague can watch the video once and tell you what the product does and what to do next.

## Step 7 — Publish and measure

Publish the video where your audience already looks, such as a product page or onboarding email. Then watch how people use it. The guide suggests judging a new format on three separate measures: how much effort it takes to make, how viewers behave while watching, and what they do afterward, such as signing up or contacting your team.

Keep the three measures separate. A video can be cheap to make and still not lead to anyone trying the product.

You'll know it worked when you can compare the video's effort, viewing behavior and follow-up actions against what you expected.

## Common mistakes

- **Building the demo around a feature list.** The fix: go back to Step 1 and tie every scene to one task.
- **Letting the footage go stale.** The fix: when your interface changes, re-record the matching screen clip before you publish again.
- **Ending with three options.** The fix: finish with one call to action. Three choices give the viewer no clear direction.

## What this means for you

- **If you run a small business**: A short demo can answer the same question for many customers, so you do not have to repeat yourself on every call.
- **If you work on a team**: Use the three-scene outline as a template. It keeps training and sales videos focused and easier to review.
- **If you're just getting started**: Pick one simple task you already do on your computer and record it. A one-minute clip is a good first project.
- **If you already use it**: Create two versions of the same script, one for a sales audience and one for new users, and keep the footage identical. Then compare how each one performs against the three measures in Step 7.

## Wrap-up

A good product demo shows one person solving one problem, and ends with one clear step. An AI avatar can deliver the narration from a script, which makes revisions and new language versions much easier, but the screen footage still has to match the current product. Start today by writing one sentence that names your viewer and their task, then sketch the three scenes on paper.
